reading.title: The Last Note
reading.text:
For six months, Hessa had practised the same piece of music: a fast, tumbling melody that leapt from the low notes of the oud to the very highest. Tonight she would play it alone, on the stage of the school’s concert hall, in front of three hundred people.
Backstage, her hands felt as though they belonged to somebody else. She flexed her fingers and tried to remember what her teacher, Mr Darwish, always said: ‘The audience is not your enemy. They want you to succeed.’
The lights dimmed. Hessa walked to the chair in the centre of the stage, sat down and began.
The first section went perfectly. The second was even better; she felt the music carrying her, the way a current carries a swimmer. Then, in the final bar, her finger slipped. The last note, the one she had practised a thousand times, came out flat and sour.
Silence. Hessa’s cheeks burned. She stared at the floor and waited for the laughter.
Instead, the hall erupted with applause. People were standing. Somewhere near the front, Mr Darwish was clapping harder than anyone.
Later, Hessa asked him why nobody had noticed her mistake. He smiled. “Everybody noticed,” he said. “But they also noticed the four minutes of beautiful music that came before it. One note does not tell the whole story.”

reading.title: Coral Reefs: Cities Under the Sea
reading.text:
Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to about a quarter of all sea creatures. For this reason, scientists often call them the rainforests of the sea.
Although coral looks like rock, or even a plant, it is actually made of tiny animals called polyps. Each polyp builds a hard, cup-shaped skeleton around itself. Over hundreds of years, millions of these skeletons join together to form a reef.
Many corals get their bright colours from microscopic algae that live inside them. The algae use sunlight to make food, which they share with the coral. In return, the coral gives the algae a safe home. This partnership is an example of symbiosis: two living things helping each other.
However, reefs are in danger. When the sea becomes too warm, the coral pushes out the algae and turns white. This is called coral bleaching. If the water cools down quickly, the coral may recover; if not, it can die.
Around the world, people are working to protect reefs. Some divers are even growing new coral on underwater frames and replanting it, piece by piece.

reading.title: The Inventor’s Apprentice
reading.text:
Nobody in the town of Al Waha had ever seen Professor Saleh smile, which was why Noor was astonished when he offered her a job.
“You fixed the clock in the square,” he said, peering at her over his spectacles. “Nobody else noticed it was running four minutes slow. I need an apprentice who notices things.”
The professor’s workshop was a maze of half-finished machines: a bicycle with wings, a teapot that sang the time and a mechanical bird with one silver eye. Noor’s first task seemed simple. She had to find out why the bird would not fly.
She tightened its springs, oiled its joints and polished its feathers. Still it sat motionless. Days passed. Noor grew frustrated, and the professor offered no help at all.
Then, late one evening, she noticed something tiny: the bird’s missing eye was not missing at all. It had been fitted the wrong way round, so that the light sensor faced inwards. When Noor turned it, the bird blinked, stretched its wings and soared to the rafters.
Behind her, someone made a strange sound. Noor turned. Professor Saleh was smiling.

reading.title: The Great Green Wall
reading.text:
Across Africa, just south of the Sahara Desert, lies a strip of land called the Sahel. For decades, the Sahel has been slowly turning into desert. Droughts, overgrazing and cutting down trees have left the soil dry and dusty, and millions of people who depend on farming have struggled to grow enough food.
In 2007, a group of African countries launched an ambitious plan to fight back: the Great Green Wall. The idea was to plant a belt of trees and plants about 8,000 kilometres long, stretching from Senegal in the west to Djibouti in the east.
The project has changed over time. Rather than a single line of trees, it has become a patchwork of green areas where local communities restore the land in ways that suit them. Farmers plant drought-resistant trees, protect young shoots that grow from old roots and dig half-moon-shaped pits that trap rainwater.
Progress has been slower than hoped, and many areas still need help. Even so, where the land has been restored, crops are growing again, wells are refilling and some families who had left are returning home.
